records.title: What Global SAR is
records.text_en: Global SAR is a 3D globe for exploring real radar observations of Earth, led by NISAR, the NASA and ISRO radar satellite. It was made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, in the challenge called Dancing with the SARs.
records.text_tr: Global SAR, Dünya'nın gerçek radar gözlemlerini keşfetmek için hazırlanmış üç boyutlu bir küredir; merkezinde NASA ve ISRO'nun radar uydusu NISAR vardır. NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026'nın Dancing with the SARs başlıklı görevi için yapılmıştır.

records.title: Who Global SAR is for
records.text_en: Global SAR is for students and teachers, journalists, people who work on disasters and the environment, and anyone curious about how our planet changes. You do not need to know anything about radar: every investigation explains what you are looking at.

records.title: What Global SAR is not
records.text_en: Global SAR is not a live emergency alert system. The investigations are the project's own analysis, not official NASA products, and every layer says whether it is an observation, a measurement the project derived or an interpretation.

records.title: What is synthetic aperture radar?
records.text_en: A radar satellite sends its own microwave pulses to the ground and records the echoes. Because it brings its own "light", it sees at night and straight through clouds and smoke.
records.text_scientific_en: SAR synthesizes a long antenna by coherently combining echoes recorded along the orbit, giving metre-scale resolution from 747 km altitude. Each pixel stores amplitude (how much energy came back) and phase (the exact distance to the ground, modulo the wavelength).

records.title: Bright and dark: backscatter
records.text_en: Bright means a lot of the pulse bounced back to the satellite. Calm water acts like a mirror and sends the pulse away, so it looks black. Buildings act like corner reflectors and look very bright. Forests are medium-bright because the canopy scatters the pulse in all directions.
records.text_scientific_en: Radar brightness (backscatter, γ⁰) depends on surface roughness relative to the wavelength, geometry (local incidence angle) and dielectric properties (moisture). Specular reflection from smooth water gives very low γ⁰; dihedral double-bounce (walls, flooded trunks) gives very high γ⁰; volume scattering in canopies is intermediate and strongly depolarizing.

records.title: Polarization: HH and HV
records.text_en: NISAR sends pulses with a horizontal wave (H) and listens for both horizontal (HH) and vertical (HV) echoes. Only messy, three-dimensional targets like tree branches flip the wave to vertical, so HV is a "vegetation detector".
records.text_scientific_en: Co-polarized HH is dominated by surface and double-bounce scattering; cross-polarized HV arises mainly from multiple scattering in volumes (canopies). The HH/HV ratio helps separate bare ground, vegetation, urban areas and flooded vegetation (HH strongly enhanced by trunk–water double bounce).

records.title: Interferometry: measuring motion
records.text_en: Compare the echo timing of two passes over the same place, 12 days apart. If the ground moved toward or away from the satellite, the echo arrives slightly earlier or later. The rainbow bands (fringes) are contour lines of that motion.
records.text_scientific_en: The interferometric phase Δφ = 4πΔR/λ links phase to line-of-sight (LOS) range change ΔR. With λ ≈ 24 cm for NISAR L-band, one 2π fringe corresponds to λ/2 ≈ 12 cm of LOS change. Phase also contains atmospheric, ionospheric and orbital terms that must be separated from ground motion.

records.title: Coherence: when the radar loses track
records.text_en: Fringes only work where the ground looks the same in both passes. Water, moving leaves or a collapsed landscape scramble the echo, and the interferogram turns into random noise there.
records.text_scientific_en: Coherence (0–1) measures the correlation of the two complex images. Water surfaces decorrelate within milliseconds; vegetation, snow, and surface disruption reduce coherence. Low-coherence pixels carry no usable phase and must be masked.

records.title: Why L-band matters
records.text_en: NISAR uses long 24 cm waves, about four times longer than Europe’s Sentinel-1. Long waves slip past leaves and reach the ground, so NISAR can measure motion and floods under forests where shorter waves fail.
records.text_scientific_en: Longer wavelength penetrates canopies and keeps interferometric coherence over vegetated and agricultural terrain for longer repeat intervals. The cost: L-band is more sensitive to the ionosphere, which adds long-wavelength phase ramps that must be estimated (e.g. by split-spectrum methods).

records.title: Venezuela earthquakes: what the radar shows
records.text_en: The default view is our measurement: how far the ground moved toward (red) or away from (blue) the satellite, in centimetres, computed from NISAR’s interferograms. BEFORE covers 1–13 June, with no earthquake: almost everything stays within a few centimetres (pale). AFTER covers 13–25 June: land south of the coast moved up to about 45 cm away from the satellite (deep blue). Black gaps are places where the radar could not get a reliable measurement (water, steep mountains, dense vegetation).
records.text_scientific_en: Derived layers (default): LOS displacement d = −φ·λ/4π (λ = 24.20 cm from centerFrequency 1239 MHz) from GUNW unwrappedPhase minus the product’s ionospherePhaseScreen, masked where coherence < 0.3 or outside connected components, referenced to a far-field box (69.1–68.7°W, 9.8–10.0°N). Both pairs share one ±50 cm colour scale. Pre-seismic pair (06-01 → 06-13): 1st–99th percentile −5.0 to +8.3 cm, standard deviation 3.5 cm, i.e. our noise floor (residual troposphere/ionosphere). Coseismic pair (06-13 → 06-25): 1st percentile −45 cm (away from the satellite), 99th +14.9 cm, standard deviation 12 cm. About half the area survives the coherence mask in each pair.

records.title: Limpopo and Incomati floods: what happened
records.text_en: In January 2026, flooding along the Limpopo and Incomati rivers in southern Mozambique inundated floodplains and farmland. NASA compared NISAR observations from 5 and 17 January to map open water.

records.title: Limpopo and Incomati floods: what the radar shows
records.text_en: The default view is our measurement of radar brightness on 5 and 17 January around Chókwè. Dark = the pulse bounced away, which is what calm water does. Pick “water mask” in the AFTER slot: bright blue = roughly 320–380 km² of new water on 17 January, mostly across the Limpopo floodplain and its irrigated fields. Muted blue = roughly 330–480 km² that was water on both dates (river channels, lakes, wetlands). The ranges come from two ways of smoothing the radar speckle. Pick “change (dB)” to see where it got darker (blue) or brighter (red).
records.text_scientific_en: Product: NISAR L2 GCOV (geocoded, terrain-flattened backscatter γ⁰), dual-pol HH/HV, track 114 ascending, frame 165. Browse composite per NISAR QA defaults: R = HH, G = HV, B = HH; each channel in linear power, clipped to its own 5th–95th percentile, gamma 0.5. Because each date is stretched independently, brightness is not comparable quantitatively between dates. Open water appears as very low backscatter in both channels (specular reflection). An HH increase relative to HV in vegetated floodplains can indicate flooded vegetation via trunk–water double bounce, which L-band detects beneath canopies.

records.title: What is SAR
records.text_en: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) is a technique that makes fine-resolution images from a radar whose own resolution is limited. The radar must be moving; it sends microwave pulses, records the echoes, and computer processing combines them as if they came from a much longer antenna.
records.text_tr: Sentetik açıklıklı radar (SAR), kendi çözünürlüğü sınırlı olan bir radardan ince çözünürlüklü görüntü üreten bir tekniktir. Radarın hareket halinde olması gerekir; mikrodalga darbeleri gönderir, yankıları kaydeder ve bilgisayar işlemesi bunları çok daha uzun bir antenden gelmiş gibi birleştirir.

records.title: Can SAR see at night

records.title: What is backscatter
records.text_en: Backscatter is the part of the transmitted radar signal that bounces back to the radar. Its strength depends mainly on the roughness and electrical properties of the surface, and is also shaped by wetness, slope, how the size of surface features compares with the wavelength, and polarization.
records.text_tr: Geri saçılım, gönderilen radar sinyalinin radara geri dönen kısmıdır. Gücü esas olarak yüzeyin pürüzlülüğüne ve elektriksel özelliklerine bağlıdır; ıslaklık, eğim, yüzey ayrıntılarının dalga boyuna göre boyutu ve polarizasyon da onu etkiler.

records.title: Why does water look dark in SAR images
records.text_en: Calm water and other smooth surfaces look black in SAR images because the radar pulse is reflected away from the spacecraft. Water roughened by wind can look bright when its waves are close in size to the radar wavelength.
records.text_tr: Durgun su ve diğer pürüzsüz yüzeyler SAR görüntülerinde siyah görünür, çünkü radar darbesi uzay aracından uzağa yansır. Rüzgârla pürüzlenen su ise dalgalarının boyu radar dalga boyuna yakın olduğunda parlak görünebilir.

records.title: What is the difference between amplitude and phase in SAR
records.text_en: Each pixel of a SAR image has an amplitude and a phase. After calibration the amplitude is proportional to how reflective the surface is, while the phase depends on the distance the wave travelled, delays in the atmosphere and a contribution from the reflecting surface.
records.text_tr: Bir SAR görüntüsünün her pikselinin bir genliği ve bir fazı vardır. Kalibrasyondan sonra genlik yüzeyin yansıtıcılığıyla orantılıdır; faz ise dalganın kat ettiği mesafeye, atmosferdeki gecikmelere ve yansıtan yüzeyin katkısına bağlıdır.

records.title: What is speckle in SAR images
records.text_en: Speckle is noise caused by the coherent nature of SAR radiation; it gives even uniform areas such as a large crop field a salt-and-pepper look. It can be reduced in several ways but is hard to remove completely.
records.text_tr: Speckle (benek gürültüsü), SAR ışınımının koherent yapısından kaynaklanan gürültüdür; büyük bir tarla gibi tekdüze alanlara bile tuz-biber görünümü verir. Çeşitli yollarla azaltılabilir, ancak tamamen gidermek zordur.

records.title: What is polarization in SAR

records.title: What is the incidence angle in SAR
records.text_en: SAR backscatter depends on the incidence angle, so the same target looks different in the near range (lower angle) and the far range (higher angle) of a swath. How strongly it changes depends on the target: flat dry soil drops off more with angle than forest does.

records.title: What is layover in SAR
records.text_en: Layover is a geometric distortion on slopes in which signals from the tops of mountains or other tall objects fall on top of other signals, so the tops appear to lean toward the sensor. Steeper slopes make it more extreme, and it shows up as bright pixels.

records.title: Can earthquakes be predicted
records.text_en: No. According to the USGS, no scientist has ever predicted a major earthquake, and it does not expect this to become possible in the foreseeable future; a real prediction would have to give the date and time, the location and the magnitude. What scientists can do is calculate the probability that a significant earthquake will occur in a given area within a certain number of years.
